title: Vizor — AI Dashboard Optimization for Tableau
summary: A local-first tool that turns a natural-language request into structured dashboard changes and applies them to the real Tableau workbook through a deterministic compiler — with schema and fidelity validation and versioned outputs, so the model plans the change but never touches the file.
problem: Editing a Tableau dashboard is fiddly, and describing the change you want in words is the natural interface. But you can't hand a workbook to an LLM and let it rewrite the XML — it can produce plausible but structurally invalid workbooks. The hard problem is getting the flexibility of natural language without losing the property that the output is only written when it passes validation.
approach: Split the responsibilities down the middle. An agent interprets the request and proposes a structured, neutral change spec (add / replace / move a visual, with grounded references) — it never sees or edits Tableau XML. Only after explicit approval does a deterministic compiler apply the change to the real workbook, through an apply loop (proposed → accepted → compiled → applied) that runs package, schema, field, zone, and fidelity validation and fails closed on any check. Outputs are written as versioned workbooks (`<source>_vizor_vN.twb`), the original's SHA-256 is verified unchanged, and every edit is undoable. It runs local-first on one machine (no cloud credentials required), with a pluggable LLM provider for planning.
outcome: A working private beta (packaged and code-signed for Windows) that produces real, versioned Tableau workbooks from planned changes — validated to still open and render, with layout fidelity scored on every generation and low-fidelity results rejected rather than shipped. Field-tested on real public dashboards. Its clearest lesson: let the model plan, and keep the correctness checks in deterministic code.

steps.title: The problem
steps.body: Describing a dashboard change in words is the natural interface — “make West region a KPI up top.” But you cannot let a language model freely rewrite a Tableau workbook's XML: it can produce plausible but structurally invalid workbooks.

steps.title: Early exploration
steps.body: The project started as a web app that took a dashboard screenshot and returned a scored, six-lens critique with a redesign plan. Useful, but it stopped at advice — it never touched the real workbook, so it couldn't actually make the change.

steps.title: The pivot
steps.body: To actually apply changes, the architecture had to change. The insight: never let the model edit the file. Let it interpret intent and propose a structured, neutral change spec, and move all correctness-critical work into deterministic code.

steps.title: The apply loop
steps.body: An agent proposes a change (add / replace / move a visual); you approve it; a deterministic compiler applies it to the workbook through a state machine — proposed → accepted → compiled → applied — that runs package, schema, field, zone, and fidelity validation and fails closed on any check.

steps.title: Safeguards
steps.body: Outputs are versioned workbooks (`<source>_vizor_vN.twb`); the original's SHA-256 is verified unchanged; every edit is undoable; and each generation is scored for layout fidelity, with low-fidelity results rejected instead of shipped. The model plans; deterministic code writes the file only after those checks pass.

steps.title: What I learned
steps.body: The best AI architecture is usually not “use the model for everything.” Use probabilistic systems where interpretation and judgment add value, and deterministic software wherever correctness is non-negotiable — the boundary between them is the product.
